records.name: Ad-Hoc Design
records.definition: Designing by improvisation with no deliberate structure or review, so the architecture accretes inconsistently.

records.name: Ad-Hoc Pattern Mixing
records.definition: Combining unrelated design patterns arbitrarily with no coherent rationale, producing an inconsistent structure.

records.name: Analysis Overhead
records.definition: The degree to which analyzing the impact of every change before making it adds effort and slows delivery.

records.name: Architecture Criteria
records.definition: The requirement that explicit criteria define what a review judges an architecture against.

records.name: Architecture Drift
records.definition: Gradual divergence of an implementation from its intended architecture as unreviewed changes accumulate.

records.name: Architecture Foundation
records.definition: The degree to which a system rests on a sound, deliberately designed architectural base rather than accreted structure.

records.name: Architecture Rules
records.definition: The requirement that explicit, checkable rules govern how the architecture may be structured and evolved.

records.name: Assumption-Based Judgment
records.definition: Judging an architecture from untested assumptions instead of measured evidence, yielding unreliable conclusions.

records.name: Attribute Scenarios
records.definition: A concrete scenario specifying how a quality attribute should hold under defined conditions and stimuli.

records.name: Automated Architecture Compliance
records.definition: The ability to verify conformance to architectural rules automatically rather than by manual review.

records.name: Blind Change
records.definition: Changing a system without analyzing what the change affects, so unintended consequences go unseen.

records.name: Change Safety
records.definition: The degree to which a change can be made with confidence that its effects are understood and contained.

records.name: Clean Boundary Design
records.definition: The ability to define clear component boundaries from the outset, free of legacy entanglement.

records.name: Competing Attributes
records.definition: The degree to which improving one quality attribute forces a trade-off against another.

records.name: Consequences
records.definition: A recorded account of the trade-offs and downstream effects that follow from an architectural decision.

records.name: Continuous Improvement
records.definition: Iteratively refining a system's design in small, ongoing steps rather than in large infrequent overhauls.

records.name: Controlled Architecture Evolution
records.definition: The ability to let an architecture change over time within deliberate guardrails rather than drifting freely.

records.name: Criteria
records.definition: The requirement that explicit, agreed measures define how an assessment reaches its verdict.

records.name: Current State
records.definition: A conceptual representation of how a system is presently structured and behaves, used as the baseline for analysis.

records.name: Decision

distinctFrom.reason: The decision records what was chosen, while the consequences record what follows from choosing it.

records.definition: A recorded architectural choice capturing what was chosen and the context in which it was made.

records.name: Decision History
records.definition: The ability to trace why past architectural choices were made by consulting their recorded rationale.

records.name: Defect Detection
records.definition: The ability to find defects in a change before it is merged or shipped.

records.name: Design Criteria
records.definition: The requirement that explicit criteria define what a design review evaluates a proposal against.

records.name: Direct-to-main Unreviewed Change
records.definition: Pushing changes straight to the main branch with no review, so unvetted code lands directly in production.

records.name: Documentation Maintenance
records.definition: The degree to which keeping decision records current adds ongoing upkeep effort.

records.name: Early Defect Prevention
records.definition: The ability to catch design flaws during review before they are built into the system.

records.name: Early Delivery with Guardrails
records.definition: The ability to ship a minimal architecture quickly while keeping essential safeguards in place.

records.name: Easier Refactoring
records.definition: The ability to restructure code more safely because consistent patterns make change predictable.

records.name: Essential Quality Attributes
records.definition: The requirement that the few quality attributes critical to viability be satisfied before any others.

records.name: Fit-for-Purpose Architecture
records.definition: The ability to shape an architecture to the problem it solves rather than to convention.

records.name: Future Scalability
records.definition: The degree to which a design can grow to meet higher future demand without rework.

records.name: Governance Discipline
records.definition: The degree to which evolving an architecture continuously demands sustained governance to prevent uncontrolled drift.

records.name: Innovation/Autonomy
records.definition: The degree to which enforcing standards constrains teams' freedom to innovate independently.

records.name: Legacy Constraints
records.definition: A binding limitation imposed by pre-existing legacy systems that a new design must accommodate.

records.name: Local Autonomy
records.definition: The degree to which enforcing architectural consistency limits individual teams' freedom to make local choices.

records.name: Local Optimization
records.definition: The degree to which enforcing shared patterns sacrifices locally optimal one-off solutions.

records.name: Manual Architecture Review Only
records.definition: Relying solely on human review to police architecture, with no automated checks, so violations slip through.

records.name: Measurable Architecture Rule
records.definition: The requirement that an architectural rule be expressed as an objective, automatically checkable measure.

records.name: Naming/Structure Conventions
records.definition: A convention of naming and structuring code uniformly across a codebase so its shape is predictable.

records.name: Operability
records.definition: The degree to which a system is easy to run, monitor, and keep healthy in production.

records.name: Predictable Evolution
records.definition: The ability to change a system with confidence that consistent structure keeps outcomes foreseeable.

records.name: Prioritized Refactoring
records.definition: The ability to rank refactoring work by assessed impact so effort targets the highest-value fixes.

records.name: Problem Decomposition
records.definition: Breaking a problem into fundamental sub-problems that can be reasoned about independently.

records.name: Quality
records.definition: The degree to which a system meets its functional and non-functional expectations.

records.name: Quality Goals
records.definition: The requirement that target levels for key quality attributes be defined for an architecture to meet.

records.name: Regression Scope Selection
records.definition: The ability to select exactly which tests a change requires by analyzing what it affects.

records.name: Remediation Planning
records.definition: The ability to plan the steps that close the gap between a system's current and target states.

records.name: Reusable Architecture Guidance
records.definition: A body of proven architectural guidance packaged for reuse across projects.

records.name: Reuse of Established Patterns
records.definition: The degree to which designing from first principles forgoes the leverage of reusing proven patterns.

records.name: Review Standards
records.definition: The requirement that agreed standards define what a code review checks for.

records.name: Risk Detection
records.definition: The ability to surface architectural risks early by reviewing structure before it is built.

records.name: Standard Patterns
records.definition: A canonical, widely agreed reusable solution that a reference architecture prescribes for a recurring problem.

records.name: Standards Definition
records.definition: A defined, authoritative set of standards that units are expected to conform to.

records.name: Target State

distinctFrom.reason: The target state is where the system is steered, while the current state is the baseline it starts from.

records.definition: A conceptual representation of the desired future structure a system is being steered toward.

records.name: Trade-Off Analysis
records.definition: The ability to weigh competing quality attributes and choose a balanced compromise between them.

records.name: Tribal Knowledge
records.definition: Critical architectural knowledge held only in the developers' heads and never recorded, lost when they leave.

records.name: Uncoordinated Divergence
records.definition: Teams independently diverging from a shared reference architecture, fragmenting the system into incompatible variants.

records.name: Unbounded Variation
records.definition: Allowing unlimited variation in how the same problem is solved, so the system sprawls into inconsistent one-offs.

records.name: Unknown Requirements
records.definition: The degree to which starting on a clean slate forces early decisions while requirements are still unknown.

records.name: Unreviewed Structural Change
records.definition: Merging changes to architectural structure without review, letting unvetted design decisions into the system.

records.name: Incremental Change
records.definition: The requirement that a system evolve in small, reversible increments rather than large risky leaps.

records.name: Rule Maintenance
records.definition: The degree to which keeping fitness-function rules current adds ongoing upkeep effort.

records.name: Undefined Target
records.definition: Attempting to close a gap toward a goal that was never clearly defined, so progress cannot be judged.

records.name: Delete After Evidence
records.definition: A technique for removing code once measurement shows nothing calls it.

records.name: Deprecation Plan
records.definition: A technique for recording for each obsolete path its owner, its replacement and its removal date.

records.name: Assign Owner
records.definition: A technique for recording a named owner for each module, risk or rule, who decides on its changes.

records.name: Severity Classification
records.definition: A technique for ranking each finding or risk on a declared scale that sets how soon it is handled.

records.name: Mitigation Plan
records.definition: A technique for recording the actions that reduce a risk, with an owner and a date for each.

records.name: Accepted Risk Record
records.definition: A technique for recording a decision to accept a risk with who accepted it and when it is reviewed again.

records.name: Scheduled Review
records.definition: A technique for setting a date on which a decision, risk or exception is examined again.

records.name: Risk Register
records.definition: A technique for keeping every known risk in one list with its owner, severity, mitigation and review date.

records.name: Decision Record with Alternatives
records.definition: A technique for recording a decision together with the options rejected and the forces that decided it.

records.name: Force Analysis
records.definition: A technique for listing the pressures a design must balance before choosing a pattern for it.

records.name: Trade-Off Matrix
records.definition: A technique for scoring candidate designs against the quality attributes that matter for the decision.

records.name: Quality Scenarios
records.definition: A technique for stating each quality attribute as a stimulus, a response and a measure the design must meet.

records.name: Decision Review
records.definition: A technique for re-examining recorded decisions when the evidence behind them changes.

records.name: Vertical Slice Proof
records.definition: A technique for proving a design by building one end-to-end path through every layer before generalizing it.

records.name: Defer Generalization
records.definition: A technique for keeping concrete code until a second real variation shows what the abstraction must cover.

records.name: Validate Required Forces
records.definition: A technique for checking that a pattern in use has the boundary rules and contracts the pattern requires.

records.name: Track Rule Metrics
records.definition: A technique for counting violations of each architecture rule over time, so recurrence is visible.

records.name: Architecture Test
records.definition: A technique for expressing a structural rule, such as a dependency direction, as a test that runs in the build.

records.name: Remove Pattern Shell
records.definition: A technique for deleting the structure of a pattern whose forces are absent, leaving the plain code it wrapped.

records.name: Duplicate Until the Pattern Stabilizes
records.definition: A technique for tolerating a small duplication until enough cases exist to show the shared shape.

records.name: Measure Delivery Cost
records.definition: A technique for measuring the time and effort an abstraction adds to delivering a change.

records.name: Anchor to Use Cases
records.definition: A technique for justifying each component by a concrete use case it serves.

records.name: Contextual Pattern Selection
records.definition: A technique for choosing a pattern by the forces of the problem at hand instead of by familiarity.

records.name: Dead Code Check
records.definition: A technique for failing the build on exports and branches that nothing reaches.

records.name: Archive Reference
records.definition: A technique for keeping removed code reachable in history or an archive instead of in the live tree.

records.name: Inconsistent Conventions
records.definition: A defect in which parts of one project use different structures, formats, tools or patterns for the same kind of thing.
